pages.hook: At an American supermarket checkout, the cashier asks a few quick questions. They are always almost the same, so you can learn them once and feel calm every time.
pages.polite: Answer each question in a short, friendly way: **Yes, thanks**, **Paper, please**, **No receipt, thanks**.

mythfact.s: The cashier often asks “Paper or plastic?”
mythfact.why: This is a very common question in US supermarkets.

mythfact.s: Many US stores have self-checkout machines.
mythfact.why: Customers scan and pay by themselves.

mythfact.s: You can only pay with cash at a supermarket.
mythfact.why: Most stores accept cards, and many accept phone payments too.

mythfact.s: In every US city, plastic bags are free.
mythfact.why: Some cities and states limit plastic bags or charge a small fee.

mythfact.s: You must say a full long sentence to the cashier.
mythfact.why: Short answers like “Paper, please.” are normal and polite.

decode.q: What do you do with your card?
decode.why: The sign says “Please insert your card”.

compare.br: In Brazil the cashier often asks “CPF na nota?” and then puts everything in plastic bags.
compare.us: In the USA the cashier often asks “Paper or plastic?”, and you say your choice in one or two words.
compare.tip: Answer the question you hear: paper, plastic, card, cash, receipt.
compare.ask: What does the cashier ask you where you live? Say one question in English.

quiz.q: The cashier asks, “Paper or plastic?” You say…
You want to use your card. You ask…
quiz.why: Can I pay by card? is the natural question.

quiz.q: “Do you want the receipt?” You do not need it. You say…
quiz.why: No, thanks. is short and polite.

pages.title: Cultural spotlight
Reading quest — Sold out at the checkout!
text: Last Friday, I went to a big store in **San Diego**. It was a sale day, a bit like **Black Friday**, the sales day after Thanksgiving in the United States. Many things were **sold out**. “Selling like hotcakes!” said a man next to me.
I wanted a blue backpack, but the shelf was empty. A worker said, “Sorry, it is **out of stock**.” I said, “**Put me on the list**. Call me when it arrives.” He smiled and wrote my phone number.
Then I went to the checkout. The line was long. Victor, the cashier, said, “Hi! **Did you find everything?**” I said, “Yes, thanks.” He asked, “**Paper or plastic?**” “Paper, please,” I said.

My bag cost twenty-three dollars and fifty cents. I asked, “**Can I pay by card?**” “Yes,” said Victor. “**Insert your card here.**” I pushed the card into the machine and waited. Beep! Then he asked, “Do you want the receipt?” “Yes, please,” I said, because I wanted to keep it.
“**Have a great day!**” said Victor. I said, “You too!” There was a self-checkout next to us, but I like to talk to a real person. A little talk makes shopping nicer.
At home, I looked at my receipt. The total was right. Now I know how a checkout works in English.
